I realize that this posting is a few years old but wanted to comment as the trend toward lean, crisp chardonnays doesn't show many signs of easing up. Much like the OP, I love a big, buttery Chard. I certainly agree that in the late 80's/early 90's vintners were getting pretty carried away with oakiness. Lindeman's Bin 65 comes to mind as a wine that was pretty much a wallop in the face with an oak stump. Other's however were producing some very tasty and enjoyable wines in a truly distinct style. When I shop whites, the selection with crisp, floral, tangy, minerally and fruity characteristics are unlimited. What's in sad scarcity are big, bold, rich wines and I miss them. Reds are well accepted across the board from bright & fruity to big, bold, juicy & spicy. Why are we so adverse to a more broad flavour continuum within white wines? At the risk of being labelled tasteless, I'm going on record as one who's waiting for the resurgence of the creamy chardonnay.

Gun show loophole? No such loophole exists. Everyone who purchases a firearm at a gun show booth fills out the same BATF form 4473 and undergoes the same FBI background check as if they were in a gun shop making the purchase. A call is made to the FBI right from the booth and the information on the form is sent. The buyer's ID is checked and sent. The FBI performs their check and responds with either "Proceed", "Hold" or "Deny". Any response other than "Proceed" and the buyer cannot complete the transaction and is sent home empty handed. The ONLY case where a background check is not required for purchases is a private transaction between two parties (ex: I sell you my gun) and those can occur anywhere. Even then many gun owners will use the same techniques gun stores do to determine a buyer's eligibility when conducting a private sale. by the way, any law requiring a BG check for private purchase is unenforceable. Even the FBI says so.

Even if you accept the premise behind the "Laffer curve", that means there is some tax rate which optimises between raising corporate taxes and not suppressing business activity. So, even in that paradigm pushed by Reagan, there is a point where cutting tax rates will lower revenues. Clearly pushing them to 0% will raise precisely 0$. And that is a very simple-minded model. There is a ton of economics research on this question. So to frame it as a "simple fact" based on "empirical evidence" that cutting tax rates always leads to more revenue is just too black and white a view of the world. As with just about everything in public policy, the truth lies in the messy complicated grey zone.

Fires have three basic modes of heat transfer - convective, radiative and conductive. Convective is mostly up through the plume (usually accompanied with particles, creating smoke). Radiative (meaning similar to the sun's rays) is usually outward from the flames, with most of it ending up in a quasi-horizontal pathway. Conductive is directly back to the burning surface or to any adjoining material (the tanker truck, in this case, for example). All three have a downward component that is a small fraction (generally less than 10%) of the overall heat release of the flame. What the train passengers felt would be many multiple times what the bridge was receiving. As a result of that natural phenomenon, you can get melting of a surface (similar to candles melting...or the asphalt in this case), but wouldn't get enough energy to cause spalling of concrete or structural loss in steel. The elevated highway section is likely fine - but CDOT would have had structural engineers look at it.

I presume this type of hearing is virtually identical to "preliminary hearings" in Canada. On that assumption, the hearing can be perfunctory or protracted depending on the disposition of the defense. The specific purpose is to determine is there is sufficient evidence against the accused to warrant of full trial. If the defense simply wants to get on with the trial, it is perfunctory; but if the defense figures it has a shot at a dismissal--a ruling that there is insufficient evidence, then the hearing can be protracted. I think part of the strategy of making that decision it the degree to which (1) the defense wants to have a overview of the prosecution's argument (the prosecutions evidence is per force given to the defense), and (2) the defense is willing to expose it's case in the pursuit of a dismissal prior to trial.

In general, police officers, like citizens, must use the minimum force reasonably necessary under the circumstances to accomplish their lawful aim. "Weapon" is not a legally precise term. Having lived in Canada and the UK, I've always found the US Memorial Day an interesting contrast to Remembrance Day in the rest of the Anglosphere. The latter is always held on 11 November (Armistice Day, marking the end of WW1). Red poppies are worn, commemorating those who died in war (see the poem, "In Flander's Fields"). Solemn ceremonies are held at national and local war memorials, where the names of the dead are inscribed, followed by a march by of living veterans from all wars. In the UK, the night before is marked by a national remembrance service, attended by political leaders and royals alike, which does not shy away from describing, to a national audience, the human costs of war. Remembrance Day in Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and the UK is a far more serious event than US Memorial Day (when we honor our war dead) and US Veterans Day (when we honor those who served). Perhaps we should align with the rest of the Anglosphere to regain their meaning.

When you have vast stands of even-aged lodgepole pine that is dead there is really no option other than clearcutting (or fire). Horse logging is, by its nature, small-scale and impracticable on a large scale and the often steep slopes around Jasper/ Banff (and I have monitored horse-logging operations). The lodgepole pine stands in these national parks are now very heavily hit by mountain pine beetle ( I viewed them this year as I drove down the icefields parkway) and they will burn eventually. This is a natural cycle and part of lodgepole pine's "strategy" to maintain itself in the ecosystem (it is a pioneer species, and wouldn't be there without fire). The stands will naturally regenerate to mainly pine.

Referring to the first referendum as having failed should include the note that it only failed because the threshold for success was set at 60%. On the question of electoral reform, though, there's a serious complicating factor that this article doesn't mention, namely, that unless the BC Liberals elect one of their own as speaker, a hypothetical NDP/Green alliance does not have the votes to pass electoral reform legislation on their own. Tradition typically dictates that in the event of a tie the speaker vote for the continuation of debate (if it's not a final passage) or for the status quo. So an NDP/Green speaker probably would not be able to supply the deciding vote to pass a law that was otherwise 43-43. If the NDP or the Greens had even one more seat, it would be a very different situation.

I've designed and completed numerous old growth pine restoration projects in several western states. Without reducing the younger in-growth crowding, largely a product of a century of active fire suppression, the old pines will lose out in the competition for moisture and nutrients. However, as with many Forest Service logging operations, the devil is in the details. Will the FS find a market for the many small trees without "sweetening the pot" with larger, older ones? Will the fragile soils be impacted by heavy handed yarding? Will currents or gooseberries be introduced into the logging created openings, the co-host for the white pine blister rust, also lethal to sugar pines? The best old growth pine restoration projects I've seen avoided logging to thin the in-growth, relying instead on cutting, lopping, and scattering of excessive in-growth around old pines followed by prescribed burning. This successful technique can be seen along Hwy. 20 near Sisters.

A clear distinction is drawn in both systems between moral obligations and legal ones. They both have means of promulgation, interpretation and enforcement through courts. They have systems of study and conferring of degrees. There is no need to “ban” canon law where it requires disobedience to civil law, because civil law effectively does that. If canon law requires bishops to break the civil law, they will still be punished by the civil legal system if they do. Bishop Pican in France is a good example.

Once they hatch and reach the correct size, they are released back into the water(creek) and swim they into the Pacific Ocean or sea water to live (and die) until it's time to spawn. There ultimately is no conclusion on where MH17 was shot down from, but there is also no credible source claiming that it was shot down from East Ukraine. In 2009, the U.S. DOL commissioned a study of the gender wage gap. The report of that study is available at http://commons.wikimannia.org/images/Gender_Wage_Gap_Final_Report_2009.pdf. In summary: more women work part time than men so they earn less; more women leave the workforce to take care of their families and when they return to work have less work experience to justify higher salaries; more women choose jobs with flexible schedules and lower wages; and more women choose jobs in low-wage industries such as child care. Once the study adjusted for all these factors, the wage gap was not 30 or 40 percent, it was closer to 5 to 7%. In addition, the national data available makes it difficult or impossible to compare apples to apples such as wages earned by men vs. women in the same job. Bottom line, while there is likely still discrimination by some employers (which is illegal) most of the wage gap is explained by factors of education, experience, and worker choice.

So you can't just look at a symptom and assume that a particular virus is the cause of that symptom, and then assume that the virus will behave the same way no matter where you find it. There is so much we still don't know. We need more research.

This lower power allows for a smaller, lighter frame and barrel, making the weapon more portable and concealable, but at the expense of accuracy and range. Examples of submachine guns include the H&K MP5, UZI, and the TEC-9. Examples of assault rifles include the AK47, M16, and Tavor. Possession of a prohibited firearms without a license AND registration certificate is an indictable offence, punishable by up to 10 years imprisonment.
